author: Claude (EFL materials writer role), v2 against the quality gate
basis: Rewritten against the v2 quality gate and the grammatical-range check. A2 and B1 were one text with synonyms swapped (vocabulary overlap 0.63, against a ceiling of 0.34 on average), and the B2 climbed by vocabulary rather than by structure, so each slide was re-conceived at each level - the same fact approached from a different angle with different content words - instead of paraphrased down or up. Every fact, name and number of the source is kept (2030 on slide 19 is the mission's only number). Facts corrected, with the reason: slide 3, the workbook B2's 'Margaining either group' is not a word, read as 'marginalising' and written so; slide 7, 'statistics confirm that professional female athletes receive significantly lower remuneration and prize money than male counterparts for identical performance' is overstated as a blanket claim, because several major tournaments now pay equal prize money, so the line keeps the gap but adds that some competitions have moved to equal prizes while the training week is identical; slide 12, 'remaining silent means compliance' is the wrong word (complicity) and a slogan, replaced by the consequence - silence leaves the player to absorb the abuse alone; slide 13, 'finally granting women's tournaments the expansive global audience they rightfully deserve and can monetize' presents an unfinished shift as complete, hedged to competitions beginning to attract serious sponsors; slide 16, 'sports equity directly correlates with robust macroeconomic stability' and 'legal guarantees of inclusion inevitably maximize a nation's complete human capital' hedged to money spent on women's sport tending to repay itself, with the evidence noted as younger than the claim; slide 5, 'stifles cognitive and physical confidence' reduced to confidence in physical strength, which is what the source's own A2 and B1 lines say; slide 9, careers 'cut short' hedged; slide 10, peers 'evaluated solely on merit' de-absolutised; slide 18, the B2's 'ensuring my media consumption reflects compromising equity' is both a typo (presumably 'uncompromising') and unfalsifiable, replaced by a checkable promise - follow one team, pay for the subscription, discuss the fixtures; slide 19, 'build a truly fair sports world by 2030' reframed as the deadline the agenda names and how much closer we can pull it; slide 20, 'Thank you for listening' removed under the house rule that the speech ends on the claim, and 'Let us exit this hall' rewritten. Level is carried by syntax and lexical load, not by word count. B1 adds present perfect, first conditionals, relative clauses and 'while'/'although' linking, and stays clear of cleft and fronted structures.

slides.1: Welcome to my presentation. Today I want to approach gender equality through sport and the media, because a stadium teaches teamwork, respect and rules. Every player deserves a fair chance to compete and to shine.
slides.2: Why does any of this matter? Sport is a mirror that reflects the society around it. When broadcasters finally show successful female athletes, millions of young girls notice, and effort starts to count more than gender.
slides.3: Remember the Olympic Games. A nation only celebrates when its men and its women both stand on the podium. If we invest in only half the population, we will simply lose half of the medals.
slides.4: Sport at the top used to belong to men alone. Officials claimed that women were too weak for heavy training or long marathons. That excuse has kept female players out of major international events for decades.
slides.5: The same pattern appears in early childhood. Boys are pushed outside and told to compete noisily, while girls are expected to remain quiet and careful. Gradually, most of them simply stop trusting their own strength.
slides.6: Look at almost any school playground. The boys usually occupy the main football pitch, while the girls are squeezed into the corners. That daily arrangement teaches them that serious competition is not really theirs.
slides.7: Now let's look at the prize money. Female professionals still earn far less than the men beside them, although several tournaments have finally moved to equal prizes. Their training hours are exactly the same.
slides.8: Coaching staff tell the same story. Most head coaches, team managers and referees are men, which means that nobody at the table has to think about women's injuries or women's health.
slides.9: The working day does not end at the stadium gate. Athletes still go home to the chores and the family expectations. If nobody at home shares that load, a promising career will simply finish early.
slides.10: Genuine change begins with the language we choose. If you use "you play like a girl" as an insult, you have already informed your classmate that she does not belong. Simple encouragement usually works much better.
slides.11: Fairness can be practised at school every week. If the courts and the equipment are shared equally, mixed teams will form naturally. Children then learn to judge each other by skill rather than gender.
slides.12: Sideline jokes are never harmless. If you hear one aimed at a female player, answer it immediately, because the silence around a joke is what makes the next one easier.
slides.13: Streaming has changed the whole picture. Women's basketball, tennis and football now reach a global crowd that old television never gave them, and that crowd is still growing quickly.
slides.14: Sports science has joined the effort as well. Wearable trackers now allow a player to monitor her own heart rate, sleep and recovery. Training can then be adjusted long before a serious injury happens.
slides.15: Social media has handed the microphone to the players. They publish their daily training, their injuries and their victories. If you share one of those videos today, you quietly widen the audience for every player.
slides.16: Several countries have now put equal pay into law for their national squads. Politicians argue that supporting women's sport brings money back to the whole economy. The early figures tend to agree with them.
slides.17: So where has this journey actually taken us? We have seen ancient traditions, unequal prize money and unpaid work at home. We have also seen streaming, wearable data and new legislation pushing the other way.
slides.18: This is my own personal promise. From tonight I will follow at least one women's football team and celebrate whenever they play. Could everybody in this room decide on one similar promise before tonight ends?
slides.19: Nobody should expect the culture to change overnight. The goals have set 2030 as the deadline, and if our generation keeps pushing, equal play can move much closer to normal.
slides.20: SDG 5 is a mission for everybody in this hall. When the playing field is genuinely level, the whole tournament improves, and the spectators get a better game. I have already picked my side.
